chapter.title: Waves and Sound
chapter.scopeNote: Original condensed MCAT Physics, Mathematics and Research Reasoning lessons. Models and calculations use stated assumptions. Independent scientific review is pending; this is not exhaustive textbook coverage.

steps.text: A periodic wave is described by amplitude, wavelength, frequency and period. Frequency is inverse period, and wave speed is v = fλ for the specified wave and medium.
Amplitude measures disturbance size, not the distance between successive crests. Wavelength is a spatial period, while ordinary period is a time interval.
Superposition adds displacements when the medium behaves linearly. Interference can enhance or cancel the local disturbance without implying that all energy has disappeared.
Standing waves arise from suitable counterpropagating waves. Boundary conditions determine nodes, antinodes and allowed wavelengths, so endpoint type matters.

steps.text: Sound in air is a longitudinal pressure wave. Air parcels oscillate about equilibrium while the disturbance transports energy through the medium.
Sound speed depends on the medium and conditions. Frequency is set by the source; crossing into a different stationary medium generally changes speed and wavelength while preserving frequency.
Sound intensity level is β = 10 log10(I/I0) in decibels. A 10 dB increase means ten times the intensity, not ten times the pressure amplitude.
For an approaching source and observer, the classical Doppler effect generally raises observed frequency. Use a stated sign convention and distinguish source speed from wave speed in the medium.
